<Card title="In this chapter — about 25 minutes" icon="sparkles">
  - **“Just read this screenshot”** — the request that breaks a text-only system
  - **Watch a picture become tiles** — in a moving picture
  - **The document whose meaning is a diagram** — and what your text pipeline did to it
  - **Send an image and a question together** — in about fifteen lines
</Card>

<Tabs>
  <Tab title="🟢 Layer 1 — Ground">
    **New to all of this?** This layer is yours. No assumptions — every term is discovered the moment you need it.

{/* STORY */}
{/* TERM LADDER: modality → multimodal model → image tokens → OCR → transcription */}

### "Just read the screenshot"

Your assistant works. Then a customer does the most natural thing in the world: instead of
describing the error, they paste a **screenshot** of it.

And your system — every clever thing you have built — has nothing. It reads text. This is a
picture. A user who has just done the most helpful thing they could think of gets told the
assistant cannot help.

The same wall appears everywhere real work does: an invoice that arrives as a scan, a contract
whose crucial detail is in a table, an architecture diagram in a PDF, a voice note from a customer
who was driving.

### How a model that only reads numbers can see

Remember Week 25's door machine: your sentence is cut into pieces and each piece becomes a
numbered tile, because the model only ever handles numbers.

An image goes through the *same idea*. It is cut into small square patches — a grid across the
picture — and each patch is turned into a list of numbers, exactly like the map positions from
Week 25 Module 2. Those patch-numbers are placed into the same sequence as your text tiles.

That is what **multimodal** means, and it is far less exotic than it sounds: **one model, one
sequence, several kinds of input**. The word "modality" just means a *kind* of input — text,
image, audio. A multimodal model accepts more than one and treats them as the same stream once
they are numbers.

Which is why you can send a picture and a question *together* and get an answer that refers to
both. Nothing new was invented; the same machine was fed something else.

### Not everything should be a picture

Here is the practical judgement that separates people who use this well from people who burn
money with it.

Images are expensive. A single high-resolution screenshot can cost as many tiles as several pages
of text, and they are slower. So the question is never "can the model see this?" — it usually can
— but **"is the meaning in the pixels, or only in the text?"**

- A scanned invoice where you need five fields → the meaning is *text* that happens to be in an
  image. Extracting the text first (**OCR** — optical character recognition, the old, cheap,
  well-understood technology for turning a picture of words into words) is usually faster,
  cheaper, and easier to check.
- A screenshot of a broken UI, a chart, a photograph of a damaged part, a diagram → the meaning
  genuinely *is* the pixels. Send the image.

The same applies to sound: a voice note is speech, and **transcription** turns it into text — after
which everything you built in this course works unchanged.

### The document your pipeline quietly ruined

This is the one that catches RAG systems, and it is worth remembering before Module 1.

Week 27 turns documents into text and cuts them into chunks. Run a technical PDF through that and
watch what happens: the paragraphs survive, and the *diagram that explained the whole thing*
becomes nothing — perhaps a caption, often not even that. The table becomes a smear of numbers
with no columns.

Your retrieval will then confidently return the passage next to the diagram, and your model will
answer without ever seeing the part that mattered. Nothing errors. The answer is simply worse than
it should be, forever, and nobody investigates because nothing looks broken.

### Do it now

About fifteen lines, and it is worth running once so the idea stops being abstract.

```bash
pip install anthropic==0.40.0
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...
```

```python
# see_it.py
import base64, anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
img = base64.standard_b64encode(open("screenshot.png", "rb").read()).decode()

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=500,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64",
                                     "media_type": "image/png", "data": img}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "What error is shown, and what is the likely cause?"},
    ]}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
print("input tiles:", msg.usage.input_tokens)   # look at this number
```

Run it on a screenshot of an error, then look at that last line. That tile count is the price of
seeing, and it is the number that should decide whether an image belongs in your pipeline at all.

<Check>
**The answer to the opening question, plainly.** A model that only handles numbers can see because
**an image is cut into patches and each patch becomes numbers, placed in the same sequence as your
text tiles** — one model, one stream, several kinds of input. The judgement that matters is not
whether it *can* see but whether the meaning lives in the pixels: text trapped in a scan is
cheaper and more checkable through OCR, while a chart, a diagram or a broken screen genuinely
needs the image. And a text-only ingestion pipeline silently discards exactly the diagrams and
tables that carried the meaning.
</Check>

<Accordion title="Checkpoint — 5 questions before you continue">
1. **What does multimodal mean?** One model accepting more than one kind of input — text, images, audio — as a single sequence of numbers.
2. **How does an image enter that sequence?** It is cut into patches, and each patch becomes a list of numbers, alongside the text tiles.
3. **When should you use OCR instead of sending the image?** When the meaning is text that happens to be in a picture — a scan of a form or invoice.
4. **When must you send the image?** When the meaning is the pixels: charts, diagrams, photographs, broken interfaces.
5. **What does a text-only ingestion pipeline lose?** Diagrams and tables — the parts that often carried the answer — silently, with nothing erroring.
</Accordion>

### A pipeline that does not throw away the diagrams

The fix is not "send every page as an image" — that is slow and expensive. It is to **classify
each page and route it**:

```python
def route_page(page):
    text = page.extract_text()
    has_figure = bool(page.images) or looks_like_table(page)
    if len(text.strip()) > 200 and not has_figure:
        return "text"          # ordinary chunking (Module 2)
    if len(text.strip()) < 40 and page.images:
        return "ocr_or_vision" # a scan: OCR first, vision if OCR is poor
    return "vision"            # mixed page: describe the figure, keep the text
```

For the `vision` route, the pattern that works is **describe-then-index**: send the page image to
a multimodal model once, at ingestion time, asking for a factual description of the figure or
table; store that description as a chunk alongside the page text, with a link back to the page.
Now the diagram is searchable by meaning, you paid for the image once rather than per query, and a
citation can point a human at the actual picture.

### Cost control for images

Three habits, in order of how much they save:

1. **Resize before sending.** Most screenshots are readable at a fraction of their native
   resolution, and tile cost scales with pixels. Downscale to the smallest size at which your eval
   set still passes.
2. **Crop to the region of interest** when you know it — an error dialog, a table — rather than
   sending a whole page.
3. **Describe once, at ingestion.** Never send the same image on every query; that is Week 28's
   caching lesson arriving early and expensively.

### When to transcribe

Audio is simpler than it looks: transcribe it, then treat the transcript as text. Two details
matter in practice — keep timestamps so a citation can point at a moment in the recording, and
keep the raw audio, because a bad transcription of a critical clause is a failure you will want to
be able to check by ear.

    Vision failures are quieter than text failures. The answer looks fluent and the thing it was
    describing was never visible.

### What the model does not see

Images are downsampled and tiled before they reach the model, which means fine detail can simply
be absent. Small text in a large screenshot, a thin line on a chart, a serial number in a corner —
these disappear before any reasoning happens, and the model will answer anyway, from context.

Two practical consequences: **crop rather than shrink** when detail matters, and **ask for a
verbatim quote** ("state the exact value shown next to 'Total'") rather than an interpretation,
because a fabricated interpretation reads the same as a real one while a fabricated quote is
easier to catch.

### Resolution, tiling and the cost curve

Tile cost grows with image area, so a naive "send the full-resolution page" pipeline is often the
single largest line in a multimodal bill. Measure cost per page at two or three resolutions
against your eval set: teams routinely find the lowest tested resolution passes and costs a
fraction of what they were paying.

### Evaluating a system you cannot read

Week 31's methods apply, with one addition: for image inputs, keep a **human-written description**
of what the picture actually contains as the ground truth, and grade the answer against that. It
is the only way to distinguish "the model saw it and reasoned wrongly" from "the model never saw
it and guessed" — and those two failures need entirely different fixes.

## Hands-on

Take five real documents from your own work — at least one scan and one with a diagram — and run
them through both routes: text-only extraction, and describe-then-index. Ask the same three
questions of each. Count how many the text-only version cannot answer at all.

## Apply it at work

**For the student.** "Handles screenshots and scanned documents" is a portfolio differentiator,
because most tutorial projects are text-only and every real user has a phone camera.

**For the professional.** Check what your current ingestion does with a page that is one large
figure. If the answer is "produces an empty chunk", you have a silent quality ceiling and now know
where it is.

## Assessment

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="5 concept questions">
  1. How does an image become something a language model can process? (Cut into patches; each patch becomes numbers placed in the same sequence as text tiles.)
  2. When is OCR the better choice than sending the image? (When the meaning is text trapped in a picture — scans, forms, invoices.)
  3. Why is describe-then-index better than sending images at query time? (You pay once at ingestion instead of on every query, and the description becomes searchable.)
  4. Why does a text-only pipeline fail silently on technical PDFs? (Figures and tables vanish; retrieval returns neighbouring text and nothing errors.)
  5. What is the safest way to ask about fine detail in an image? (Ask for a verbatim quote of the value, and crop rather than shrink.)
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Coding challenge">
  Build `ingest_page(page)` that classifies a page as text, scan or figure; runs OCR on scans;
  calls a multimodal model once for figures to produce a factual description; and emits chunks with
  a `source_kind` field and a page link. Hidden tests check: a figure-only page never produces an
  empty chunk; the same image is never described twice across two runs of the same document; and
  every chunk carries a citation back to its page.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Interview questions (junior / mid / senior)">
  - **Junior:** "A user pastes a screenshot instead of the error text. What does your system do?"
  - **Mid:** "Our RAG answers are weak on technical manuals but fine on policy documents. What would you check first?"
  - **Senior:** "Design a document pipeline for mixed scans, native PDFs and photographs at 50,000 pages a month, with a cost ceiling. Explain what you route where, and how you would prove the routing is right."
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

## Common mistakes

- **Sending every page as an image.** Slow, expensive, and unnecessary for pages that are text.
- **Sending the same image on every query.** Describe it once at ingestion instead.
- **Shrinking when detail matters.** Crop instead; downsampling removes the very thing you needed.
- **Trusting an interpretation of a chart.** Ask for the exact value; fabricated quotes are easier to catch than fabricated summaries.
- **Ignoring what ingestion did to your figures.** The failure is silent and permanent until someone looks.
